Useful for team-standard workflows.
Pin and review like a GitHub Action.
Read the hooks and MCPs it adds.
Do not install random bundles on secret-bearing repos.
Smaller is better; skip the bundle if one hook is enough.

questions.q: What does a plugin package together?
questions.a: Some mix of commands, skills, hooks, subagents, and integrations, distributed as one unit.

questions.q: How do you review a plugin the way you review a GitHub Action?
questions.a: Read what programs it runs, what network it can hit, pin the version, and review upgrades in a PR.

questions.q: After installing a bundle, the agent can write to staging. Why?
questions.a: The plugin added an MCP or hook you did not read. Audit the bundle's tools and remove write access.

questions.q: When would you skip a plugin?
questions.a: When you need a single hook or command. A bundle is extra surface.

questions.q: Why pin plugin versions?
questions.a: So a silent upgrade cannot change hooks or add tools under you.

skills-that-transfer-across-agents.explain:
## What it is

Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI — the **brands** change. The **durable skills** do not: **context** (minimum useful), **specifications**, **planning**, **delegation**, **automation** (hooks), and **verification** (diff, test, review). If you only learn a slash-command syntax you will reset every six months.

Transfer means you can sit down in a new IDE and still write a spec, still restrict files, still run the test, still read the diff. The product tutorial is a thin layer.

This is the point of the whole module. The tools are examples. The loop is the skill.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job you will switch tools when the company does. Interviewers may ask "we use X, not Y — does that matter?". The senior answer is no, and then you name the six durables. The junior answer is a feature tour of last month's blog.

This is also how you stay employable in a noisy market.

## How it works + one small example

When you try a new agent, map the durables on day one:

- Where do I put standing memory?
- How do I restrict paths?
- How do I run a command?
- Is there a hook on stop?
- How do I see the diff?

Then do one small task with the verification loop. Do not spend a week on theme packs.

Write your skills in plain markdown in the repo so more than one product can read them, even if only as pasted commands.

## Failure modes

1. **Identity tied to one product.**

2. **Collecting plugins** instead of practising the loop.

3. **Skipping verification** because the new tool "is better".

4. **Repo docs that only work** with one vendor's filename.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The durable parts are context, spec, plan, delegation, automation and verification. I can move those to any coding agent. The brand is a UI. I do not skip the loop because the tool is new.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Brands change; the loop does not.
- Prove it in an artefact: Durables: context, spec, plan, delegation, hooks, verification.
- Prove it in an artefact: Map those on day one in a new tool.
- Prove it in an artefact: Keep repo instructions in plain markdown.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not skip review because the UI is slick.
- Prove it in an artefact: This module's point is transfer, not a vendor.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: The durable parts are context, spec, plan, delegation, automation and verification. I can move those to any coding agent. The brand is a UI. I do not skip the loop because the tool is new. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.
keyPoints: Brands change; the loop does not.
Durables: context, spec, plan, delegation, hooks, verification.
Map those on day one in a new tool.
Keep repo instructions in plain markdown.
Do not skip review because the UI is slick.
This module's point is transfer, not a vendor.

questions.q: Which skills transfer across coding agents?
questions.a: Minimum useful context, specs, planning, delegation, deterministic hooks, and the verify-the-diff loop.

questions.q: You must switch from tool A to tool B this week. What do you learn first?
questions.a: Where standing memory goes, how to restrict files, how to run tests, how to see the diff. Then do one small loop.

questions.q: A candidate can only describe one vendor's slash commands. What are they missing?
questions.a: The durables. Ask them to spec and verify a change without the brand names.

questions.q: How do you write project instructions that survive a tool change?
questions.a: Plain markdown in the repo: commands, layout, don'ts. Product-specific files can include it or point to it.

questions.q: Why is verification listed as durable?
questions.a: Every tool can generate wrong code. Diff, test and review are not a feature; they are the job.

reviewing-ai-generated-diffs.explain:
## What it is

Treat model output as an **untrusted pull request**. Before merge you check **tests**, **secrets**, and **edge cases** the same way you would for a stranger. The author being a model is a reason to read *harder*: invented APIs, deleted assertions, `.env` files, "helpful" refactors, license-incompatible snippets.

`git diff` is the artefact. /docs looking good is not. A green suite that the model also wrote is not enough unless you read the tests.

This is the verification loop's review step, written as a habit for generated code.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the new default: a large fraction of lines will be generated. Interviewers will ask what you look for. They want secrets, tests, scope creep, and a sentence you can say about the change. They want you to have rejected a diff.

Security teams already assume AI PRs are hostile until reviewed. Join them.

## How it works + one small example

Checklist on every generated diff:

1. Scope: only the files you asked for?
2. Secrets: keys, tokens, connection strings, prod hosts?
3. Tests: did it delete or weaken any? Are empty and error paths covered?
4. Invented APIs: do the imports exist?
5. Data: injection, missing auth, client-supplied user_id?
6. Can you explain the change in 30 seconds?

If 6 fails, do not merge. Ask for a smaller diff or write it yourself.

Use `git add -p` so you do not stage a drive-by file.

## Failure modes

1. **LGTM because it ran.**

2. **Not opening every file** in the diff.

3. **Trusting tests the model wrote** without reading them.

4. **Staging with git add .**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A generated diff is an untrusted PR. I check scope, secrets, tests, invented APIs and whether I can explain it. If I cannot explain it I do not merge it. git add -p, not git add .

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Generated code is untrusted until reviewed.
- Prove it in an artefact: Check scope, secrets, tests, invented APIs, auth.
- Prove it in an artefact: Read the tests the model wrote.
- Prove it in an artefact: Explain-it-or-reject.
- Prove it in an artefact: git add -p to avoid drive-bys.
- Prove it in an artefact: Green CI is not a review.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: A generated diff is an untrusted PR. I check scope, secrets, tests, invented APIs and whether I can explain it. If I cannot explain it I do not merge it. git add -p, not git add . The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.
keyPoints: Generated code is untrusted until reviewed.
Check scope, secrets, tests, invented APIs, auth.
Read the tests the model wrote.
Explain-it-or-reject.
git add -p to avoid drive-bys.
Green CI is not a review.

questions.q: What do you look for in an AI-generated diff before merge?
questions.a: Scope, secrets, weakened tests, invented imports, auth/injection, and whether you can explain the change.

questions.q: The suite is green but test_missing_label now asserts True. What happened?
questions.a: The model 'fixed' the test. Reject. Restore the assertion.

questions.q: Why use git add -p on generated work?
questions.a: So a drive-by file or a secret is not staged just because it is in the tree.

questions.q: Why is generated code less trusted than a teammate's?
questions.a: It invents APIs, has no reputation, and will delete tests to go green. Review harder, not lighter.

questions.q: The diff includes a 'small refactor' you did not ask for. What do you do?
questions.a: Revert that part. Ask for a separate PR if the refactor is real. Do not merge a surprise.

prompting-the-assistant-with-failing-tes.explain:
## What it is

When you ask a model to fix a failure, give it the **traceback** and the **intended assertion**, not a vague "fix it". The test name, the expected versus actual, and the command to rerun are the spec. Vague prompts produce vague rewrites.

This is the debug job with a sharp interface. The failing test is already the spec you should have written. Use it.

If there is no test, write the assertion first — even a one-liner — then paste that. Do not let the model invent the behaviour.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "fix the tests" without a paste is how you get a deleted test. Interviewers will ask how you prompt on a red CI. They want the traceback in the prompt and "do not change the assertion".

This is also the fastest loop: the model does not hunt. You already isolated the unit.

## How it works + one small example

Bad: "Tests are failing, please fix."

Good:

```
uv run pytest tests/test_tickets.py::test_empty_ticket_returns_other
AssertionError: assert None == 'other'
Traceback: ... last frame in label_of ...
Do not change the test. Make empty tickets return 'other'.
Re-run the same command.
```

If it fails again, paste the new traceback. Do not add a second feature.

If the assertion is wrong, you change the test in a separate, explained step — not the agent silently.

## Failure modes

1. **"Fix it"** with no error.

2. **Allowing the test to change** without saying so.

3. **Pasting 400 failing tests** at once.

4. **Changing the product** in the same breath as the fix.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I prompt with the traceback, the assertion, and the command. I say do not change the test. One failure at a time. The test is the spec; the model is the typist.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: Paste traceback + expected versus actual + command.
- Prove it in an artefact: Forbid silent test changes.
- Prove it in an artefact: One failure at a time.
- Prove it in an artefact: Write the assertion first if it does not exist.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not mix a feature into a fix prompt.
- Prove it in an artefact: 'Fix it' is not a spec.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. They will hand you a broken traceback, a status code, a latency number, a lockfile, or a model card and wait for the next action. Say what you look at first, what you change, and what you refuse to ship. If time is short, use this line and then add one concrete artefact: I prompt with the traceback, the assertion, and the command. I say do not change the test. One failure at a time. The test is the spec; the model is the typist.

A third trap is mixing adjacent ideas. Keep this topic's mechanism separate from nearby ones, name the trade-off, and give a number or a verb (measure, pin, retry, refuse) so the answer sounds like work, not a blog post.
keyPoints: Paste traceback + expected versus actual + command.
Forbid silent test changes.
One failure at a time.
Write the assertion first if it does not exist.
Do not mix a feature into a fix prompt.
'Fix it' is not a spec.

questions.q: Write a good fix-it prompt for a failing pytest.
questions.a: Include the command, the assertion error, the last traceback frames, the intended behaviour, and 'do not change the test'.

questions.q: Why is 'fix the tests' a bad prompt?
questions.a: It permits deleting or weakening tests. It also does not say which failure or what correct means.

questions.q: The agent made CI green by changing expected from 'other' to None. What do you do?
questions.a: Revert the test, restate the assertion as the spec, and ask for a production-code fix only.

questions.q: There is no test, only a production 500. What do you send the agent?
questions.a: A new failing test (or a snippet) that reproduces the 500, then the traceback. Do not start with 'make 500s go away'.

questions.q: How many failures do you put in one prompt?
questions.a: One, or a tight cluster with the same cause. A wall of 400 failures invites a rewrite.

app-vs-environment-vs-machine.explain:
## What it is

Three layers. The **application** is your code and its declared dependencies (`app/`, `pyproject.toml`). The **environment** is the concrete Python, packages, env vars, and files that code sees when it runs. The **machine** is the OS, kernel, CPU, and disk that host that environment — your laptop, a VM, or a container host.

A bug can live in any layer. "Works on my machine" usually means the environments differ (Python 3.12 vs 3.10, a missing env var) or the machines differ (no Postgres, different libc). Containers exist to make the **environment** a shipped artefact so the machine can be generic.

You do not ship your laptop. You ship an image of the environment plus the app.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how you talk about Docker without magic. Interviewers ask why Docker helps (same environment on laptop, CI, and prod) and what it does not do (it does not remove the need for config and secrets; it does not make a bad app correct). They ask what still differs (the machine: GPUs, disk, the host network).

They will ask where a missing `DATABASE_URL` lives (environment) versus a segfault in a wheel (often machine/glibc) versus a logic bug (app).

This split is the rest of the capstone.

## How it works + one small example

Laptop: app is the repo, environment is `.venv` + `.env`, machine is macOS.

CI: app is the checkout, environment is what `uv sync --frozen` built, machine is the runner image.

Prod: app is a COPY in a Dockerfile, environment is the image layers plus injected env vars, machine is the orchestrator's node.

A test that mocks the database tests the app. A compose stack tests the environment. A node running out of disk is the machine.

When you write a Dockerfile you are defining the environment. When you pick `python:3.12-slim` you are picking a machine-ish base that you will treat as disposable.

## Failure modes

1. **Baking laptop paths** into the app (`/Users/you/...`).

2. **Assuming the container has your .env.**

3. **Blaming Docker** for an app bug.

4. **Treating the container as the machine you SSH into forever.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

App is the code, environment is what it sees at run time, machine is the host. Docker ships a reproducible environment so the machine can be generic. I debug by asking which layer is different.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: App = code + declared deps. Environment = concrete runtime. Machine = host.
- Prove it in an artefact: Works-on-my-machine is usually environment drift.
- Prove it in an artefact: Containers ship the environment, not your laptop.
- Prove it in an artefact: Config and secrets still inject into the environment.
- Prove it in an artefact: Machines still differ (disk, GPU, network).
- Prove it in an artefact: Pick the layer before you pick the tool.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (App is the code, environment is what it sees at run time, machine is the host. Docker ships a reproducible environment so the machine can be generic. I debug by asking which layer is different) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).
keyPoints: App = code + declared deps. Environment = concrete runtime. Machine = host.
Works-on-my-machine is usually environment drift.
Containers ship the environment, not your laptop.
Config and secrets still inject into the environment.
Machines still differ (disk, GPU, network).
Pick the layer before you pick the tool.

questions.q: What is the difference between the app, the environment, and the machine?
questions.a: App is your code and declared dependencies. Environment is the concrete interpreter, packages, and env vars. Machine is the OS and hardware that host it.

questions.q: A container starts and dies with FileNotFoundError on ~/data. Which layer?
questions.a: The app assumed a laptop path (machine/user). Use an env var and a path inside the environment (e.g. /data).

questions.q: CI uses Python 3.10 and your laptop 3.12. Tests fail only in CI. Layer?
questions.a: Environment (and the base machine image). Pin requires-python and the image tag.

questions.q: What does Docker reproduce well, and what must still be injected?
questions.a: It reproduces the packaged environment. Secrets, DATABASE_URL, and machine resources are still injected or provided by the host.

questions.q: Why not ship the laptop?
questions.a: Paths, OS, extra packages, and secrets you did not declare. The next machine will not have them.

containers-images.explain:
## What it is

A **container** is a running process with its own filesystem view, isolated enough to look like a small machine. An **image** is the **immutable snapshot** that process starts from: layers of files plus a default command. You **build** an image, **run** a container from it. Many containers can run from one image.

Docker (and others) implement this with OS isolation, not a full VM per app. That is why they are fast to start and why they share the host kernel. Isolation is not a security boundary you should trust for hostile tenants without more work.

**Reproducibility** comes from the image: same layers, same app, same default env. It does not come from "I remember how I installed things".

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "it is in Docker" should mean "anyone can run this image and get the same environment". Interviewers ask image versus container (class versus instance is a fair analogy). They ask why this helps CI (CI runs the same image). They ask what is not reproducible (`latest`, unpinned base, secrets baked at build).

They may ask why not a VM (heavier, slower, still useful for a different kernel). Keep it practical.

## How it works + one small example

```
docker build -t tickets:1.2.0 .
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 --env-file .env tickets:1.2.0
```

The image `tickets:1.2.0` is the artefact you can push to a registry. The container is the running process mapping port 8000.

Change the code, rebuild the image. Do not "fix the container" with `docker exec` and walk away — that change dies with the container. If you needed it, put it in the Dockerfile.

List: `docker images`, `docker ps`. Logs: `docker logs`.

## Failure modes

1. **Mutating a running container** as the source of truth.

2. **No tag** except latest.

3. **Thinking containers are VMs** you patch forever.

4. **Assuming isolation equals security.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

writing-and-running-a-dockerfile.explain:
## What it is

A **Dockerfile** is a recipe of layers: a **FROM** base, **COPY** files, **RUN** install commands, **ENV**, **EXPOSE**, **CMD** or **ENTRYPOINT**. `docker build` executes it and tags an image. `docker run` starts a container, maps **ports** (`-p 8000:8000`), and passes **environment** (`-e` or `--env-file`).

Order matters for **cache**: copy the lockfile and install deps before copying the whole source so a code change does not reinstall the world. `.dockerignore` keeps `.venv` and `.git` out.

Secrets: pass at **run**, not `ENV KEY=real` in the Dockerfile. `EXPOSE` is documentation; `-p` is the actual publish.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is how the capstone ships. Interviewers will ask you to sketch a Dockerfile for FastAPI. They want a slim Python base, uv or pip from a lock, a non-root user if you can, CMD that runs uvicorn, and env at runtime. They will mark baking a password as a fail.

They ask why the first build is slow and the second is fast (cache) and why copying `.venv` from the laptop is wrong (wrong OS).

## How it works + one small example

```
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./
RUN pip install uv && uv sync --frozen --no-dev
COPY app ./app
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uv", "run", "uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
```

```
docker build -t tickets:1.2.0 .
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 -e DATABASE_URL -e APP_SECRET tickets:1.2.0
```

`.dockerignore`: `.venv`, `.git`, `.env`, `__pycache__`, tests if you do not need them in the image.

`--host 0.0.0.0` is required; `127.0.0.1` inside the container is not reachable from the host map.

## Failure modes

1. **COPY . .** before install, busting cache every time.

2. **CMD on 127.0.0.1.**

3. **ENV SECRET=...** in the Dockerfile.

4. **Copying .venv** from macOS into a Linux image.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A Dockerfile is layered: lockfile and install first, then source, CMD on 0.0.0.0, secrets at run. I build a tag, I map the port, I do not bake keys, and I dockerignore .venv and .env.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD are the core.
- Prove it in an artefact: Copy lockfile and install before app source for cache.
- Prove it in an artefact: Pass secrets at run, not in the image.
- Prove it in an artefact: EXPOSE documents; -p publishes.
- Prove it in an artefact: Listen on 0.0.0.0 inside the container.
- Prove it in an artefact: dockerignore .venv, .git, .env.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. They will hand you a broken traceback, a status code, a latency number, a lockfile, or a model card and wait for the next action. Say what you look at first, what you change, and what you refuse to ship. If time is short, use this line and then add one concrete artefact: A Dockerfile is layered: lockfile and install first, then source, CMD on 0.0.0.0, secrets at run. I build a tag, I map the port, I do not bake keys, and I dockerignore .venv and .env.

A third trap is mixing adjacent ideas. Keep this topic's mechanism separate from nearby ones, name the trade-off, and give a number or a verb (measure, pin, retry, refuse) so the answer sounds like work, not a blog post.

Copy lockfile and install before app source for cache.
Pass secrets at run, not in the image.
EXPOSE documents; -p publishes.
Listen on 0.0.0.0 inside the container.
dockerignore .venv, .git, .env.

questions.a: The server listens only on the container loopback. The published port forwards to the container's 0.0.0.0:8000. Bind 0.0.0.0.

questions.a: docker run -e or the platform secret, not ENV in the Dockerfile and not a copied .env.

questions.a: So dependency layers cache until the lock changes. Code edits then reuse the install layer.

questions.a: .dockerignore for .venv, .git, data dumps, and local models.

layers-logs-startup-failures.explain:
## What it is

Each Dockerfile instruction produces a **layer**. Cached layers reuse. A change invalidates that layer and all after it. **`.dockerignore`** keeps junk out of the build context. **Container logs** are the process stdout/stderr — `docker logs` or the platform's log drain. **Startup failures** are usually: wrong CMD, missing env, port not bound, import error, or the process exiting 0 by mistake.

`docker logs` is the first tool when a container **exits 1**. `docker ps -a` shows the exited container. An image that "built fine" can still fail at run; build does not run your CMD.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "CrashLoopBackOff" is this topic. Interviewers will ask what you do when a container exits 1 (logs, then CMD, then env, then port). They ask why a tiny Dockerfile change rebuilt everything (you copied source before pip). They ask where print/logging goes (stdout, so the platform can collect it).

They like "build success ≠ run success".

## How it works + one small example

Rebuild too much: you `COPY . .` then `RUN uv sync`. Swap the order.

See why it died:

```
docker ps -a
docker logs --tail 200 CONTAINER_ID
docker inspect CONTAINER_ID   # Args, Env, State.ExitCode
```

Common: `ModuleNotFoundError` (did not COPY app), `KeyError: DATABASE_URL` (env missing), `address already in use` (port), `exec format error` (wrong platform/arch).

Health: if CMD is a shell that exits, the container exits. Keep the server in the foreground. Do not daemonise inside the container.

## Failure modes

1. **Ignoring logs** and rebuilding at random.

2. **Backgrounding the server** so the container exits 0.

3. **Huge context** without dockerignore.

4. **Assuming EXPOSE means it started.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Layers cache from the top; a change busts everything below. When a container exits 1 I read logs, then CMD, env and the bind address. Build success is not run success. The server stays in the foreground.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Each instruction is a layer; order is cache.
- Prove it in an artefact: dockerignore shrinks context and avoids leaking .env.
- Prove it in an artefact: docker logs is the first step on exit 1.
- Prove it in an artefact: Build does not execute CMD.
- Prove it in an artefact: Keep the main process in the foreground.
- Prove it in an artefact: inspect shows Env and ExitCode.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: Layers cache from the top; a change busts everything below. When a container exits 1 I read logs, then CMD, env and the bind address. Build success is not run success. The server stays in the foreground. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.

questions.q: A container exits 1 immediately. What is your order?
questions.a: docker logs, then inspect CMD and env, then confirm the server binds 0.0.0.0 and required vars are set.

questions.q: Why did a one-line Python change reinstall all packages?
questions.a: The Dockerfile copied the whole tree before installing, so the install layer invalidated.

questions.q: CMD is `uvicorn ... &` and the container exits 0. Why?
questions.a: The shell's last command is the backgrounding. The main process ended. Run uvicorn in the foreground.

questions.q: Where do FastAPI logs go in Docker?
questions.a: Stdout/stderr of the main process. Use logging to stdout, then docker logs or the platform drain.

questions.q: What does dockerignore do besides speed?
questions.a: It keeps .env, .git and local junk out of the build context so they are harder to COPY by accident.

containerizing-a-fastapi-app.explain:
## What it is

To **containerize FastAPI** you put the app in an image that can **import the package**, **read config from the environment**, and **reach its services** (Postgres on another hostname, not `localhost` meaning the container). Compose or the platform provides the network and the env. The container is not your laptop: `localhost` inside is the container itself.

You typically run uvicorn (or gunicorn+uvicorn workers) as CMD. You do not run `fastapi dev` in production (it is a reload server). You mount nothing you do not need. You pass `DATABASE_URL` pointing at the db service name (`postgres://...@db:5432/app`).

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job this is the capstone. Interviewers ask why `localhost` broke in Docker (Postgres is another container). They ask how you pass config (env). They ask how you would add a second process (don't: one process per container, or a real supervisor). They ask about multi-stage builds if the image is fat.

This is the first time the HTTP module, the DB module, and the env-var module meet.

## How it works + one small example

`docker-compose.yml` sketch:

```
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://app:app@db:5432/app
    depends_on: [db]
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_DB: app
```

The app uses `db` as the hostname. Migrate in an entrypoint or a one-shot job, not by hand on the laptop only.

Health: a `/health/ready` that SELECT 1s the database so the platform does not send traffic early.

## Failure modes

1. **DATABASE_URL=localhost** inside the api container.

2. **fastapi dev** as the production CMD.

3. **SQLite file** on the container filesystem and wondering where it went.

4. **Two responsibilities** in one container without a plan.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I image the FastAPI app, inject env, and point DATABASE_URL at the db service name, not localhost. Production CMD is uvicorn in the foreground. Ready checks wait for the database. One process per container.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: localhost inside the container is the container.
- Prove it in an artefact: Use the compose service name as the DB host.
- Prove it in an artefact: Production CMD is uvicorn, not fastapi dev.
- Prove it in an artefact: Config via environment; migrate as a job or entrypoint.
- Prove it in an artefact: Ready check hits the database.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not store durable data on the container filesystem.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: I image the FastAPI app, inject env, and point DATABASE_URL at the db service name, not localhost. Production CMD is uvicorn in the foreground. Ready checks wait for the database. One process per container. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

questions.a: localhost is the API container, not the host or the db container. Use the service name and the Docker network.

questions.a: Two services, DATABASE_URL host=db, depends_on or a real wait-for-ready, api publishes 8000.

questions.a: It is a development server with reload. Use uvicorn/gunicorn as the process.

questions.a: The container filesystem is ephemeral. Use Postgres (or a volume, if you really must) for durable data.

deploying-to-a-public-url.explain:
## What it is

**Deploy** means a platform runs your image (or a buildpack) and gives you a **public HTTPS URL**. Examples: a VM with Docker, Fly, Render, Cloud Run, a Kubernetes Service. You push an image or a git SHA; the platform injects env, maps 443 to your port, and restarts if the process dies.

The public URL is the contract you verify with curl and `/docs`. DNS, TLS, and the platform's router are extra hops. A local `localhost:8000` is not a deploy.

You still owe health checks, logs, and secrets. The platform does not make the app correct.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The Level 0 capstone requires a URL someone else can hit. Interviewers will ask how you would deploy a container (pick a platform, set env, map the port, curl the URL). They will ask what differs from local (HTTPS, real DNS, secrets, scale-to-zero cold starts).

They may ask how you would roll back (redeploy the previous tag). That is why you pin tags.

## How it works + one small example

Path: build `tickets:1.2.0`, push to a registry, create a service with port 8000, set `DATABASE_URL` and secrets, attach a Postgres add-on, run migrations, assign a hostname.

Verify:

```
curl -sS https://tickets.example.com/health/ready
curl -sS https://tickets.example.com/docs
```

If the platform sleeps the app, the first request is slow — say so in the README.

Do not expose Postgres to the world. Only the API URL is public.

## Failure modes

1. **Calling localhost a deploy.**

2. **Public database.**

3. **No HTTPS** on a real hostname (or ignoring the platform cert).

4. **No rollback plan** because you only have latest.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A deploy is a public HTTPS URL running a pinned image with injected secrets. I verify with curl and /docs, I keep the database private, and I can roll back by redeploying the previous tag.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: Public URL + HTTPS is the deploy; localhost is not.
- Prove it in an artefact: Platform injects env and maps 443 to your port.
- Prove it in an artefact: Pin an image tag so you can roll back.
- Prove it in an artefact: Verify with curl and /docs.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not expose Postgres.
- Prove it in an artefact: Cold starts and extra hops are real.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: A deploy is a public HTTPS URL running a pinned image with injected secrets. I verify with curl and /docs, I keep the database private, and I can roll back by redeploying the previous tag. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.

questions.a: HTTPS URL, /health/ready, /docs or a curl of a real endpoint, and that secrets are not the laptop's.

questions.q: Why is localhost not a deploy?
questions.a: Nobody else can reach it, there is no public TLS, and it does not prove the image runs on a generic machine.

questions.a: Redeploy the previous image tag (or git SHA). You cannot roll back if you only ever pushed latest.

production-env-vars-secrets.explain:
## What it is

**Production configuration** is environment variables and **secrets** that are **not** the ones on your laptop. The platform injects them. You keep a `.env` for local and a secret store for prod. You never copy prod secrets to your laptop "to test". You never bake them in the image.

Split **config** (log level, feature flags) from **secrets** (DB password, API keys) if the platform does. Both arrive as env in a typical small app. Rotation is a new value + restart. Audit who can read the store.

`DEBUG=true` in production is a leak. `CORS_ORIGINS=*` with credentials is a leak. Defaults in code that point at localhost will silently mis-wire.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, using the local `.env` in prod (or vice versa) is a classic outage or leak. Interviewers ask how prod gets `DATABASE_URL` (platform secret) versus how you get it (gitignore .env). They ask what you do on a leak (rotate, restart, scan logs).

They ask how you prevent the image from containing a secret (no ENV, no COPY .env, dockerignore).

This is the deploy half of the credentials topic.

## How it works + one small example

Local: `.env` + compose `--env-file`. Prod: platform UI or IaC sets `DATABASE_URL`, `APP_SECRET`. Same names, different values.

Settings class: required fields, no localhost default in the production image. Fail boot if missing.

Promote a new secret: add it, deploy, drop the old. Do not log Settings().model_dump() if it includes secrets — mark those fields and redact.

A staging environment is a third set of values, not prod copies.

## Failure modes

1. **COPY .env** into the image.

2. **DEBUG=true** in prod.

3. **Laptop URL in the platform** "just to get it up".

4. **Logging the full settings object.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Prod env vars and secrets are a different set, injected by the platform, never baked into the image and never copied from my laptop. I fail boot if they are missing, I rotate on leak, and I do not log them.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: Same names, different values per environment.
- Prove it in an artefact: Platform secret store, not a copied .env.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not bake secrets into the image.
- Prove it in an artefact: No unsafe defaults that silently run in prod.
- Prove it in an artefact: Rotate + restart on leak.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not log the settings dump.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. They will hand you a broken traceback, a status code, a latency number, a lockfile, or a model card and wait for the next action. Say what you look at first, what you change, and what you refuse to ship. If time is short, use this line and then add one concrete artefact: Prod env vars and secrets are a different set, injected by the platform, never baked into the image and never copied from my laptop. I fail boot if they are missing, I rotate on leak, and I do not log them.

A third trap is mixing adjacent ideas. Keep this topic's mechanism separate from nearby ones, name the trade-off, and give a number or a verb (measure, pin, retry, refuse) so the answer sounds like work, not a blog post.

questions.q: How do production secrets get into the process?
questions.a: The platform injects them as environment variables or mounted files from a secret store. The image does not contain them.

questions.q: The image has a real DATABASE_URL because you COPY .env. What now?
questions.a: Rotate the password, rebuild without that file, dockerignore .env, scan the registry for the old image.

questions.q: Why not reuse prod secrets in staging?
questions.a: A staging leak becomes a production leak. Use a third set of values.

questions.q: What should happen if APP_SECRET is missing at boot?
questions.a: The process should exit. A default is how you ship an insecure service.

questions.a: Rotate, redact the logger, purge what you can, treat the log store as leaked.

health-checks-and-readiness.explain:
## What it is

**Liveness** means the process is alive (not deadlocked). **Readiness** means it can take traffic (database is up, migrations applied, warm-up done). Platforms probe these endpoints and **stop sending traffic** if ready fails, and **restart** the container if live fails.

A `/health/live` that always returns 200 if the process can serve HTTP is enough for liveness. A `/health/ready` that `SELECT 1`s Postgres (and any must-have dependency) is readiness. If you only have one probe, make it readiness — or you will receive traffic while the DB is down and serve 500s.

Do not make the ready check so heavy it becomes the outage.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, this is why Kubernetes/Cloud Run/Load balancers do not send users to a booting task. Interviewers ask live versus ready. They ask what you would check (DB, not disk-full unless you mean it). They ask what happens if ready is too strict (flapping) or too loose (500s).

They will mark a deploy without probes as incomplete for the capstone.

## How it works + one small example

```
@app.get("/health/live")
def live() -> dict:
    return {"status": "ok"}

@app.get("/health/ready")
def ready(db=Depends(get_db)) -> dict:
    db.execute(text("SELECT 1"))
    return {"status": "ok"}
```

Platform: ready probe on `/health/ready`, interval 5s, fail after a few. Start period long enough for boot and migrate.

Do not require a vendor LLM in ready unless the product cannot work without it. You will take the whole site down when the vendor blinks.

Auth: health endpoints are usually public but boring. Do not put secrets in the response.

## Failure modes

1. **One probe that only checks the process** — traffic during DB outage.

2. **Ready depends on a flaky third party.**

3. **Heavy ready** (full migration, huge query).

4. **No start grace** so the task is killed while migrating.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Live means the process is up; ready means it can take traffic. I expose both, I SELECT 1 the database on ready, and I do not depend on a flaky vendor. The platform uses ready to hold traffic during boot.

## A merge-ready drill

Turn the note into something you would accept in a PR. Name the file, header, query, or eval item you would add. Say who gets paged if it is wrong. Then actually do the smallest version of that check: run the test, print the SQL, count the tokens, or open the generated OpenAPI path. Knowledge that never touches an artefact decays into slogans.

Walk the key points as if you were reviewing someone else's change:

- Prove it in an artefact: Liveness: process is not dead. Readiness: safe to send traffic.
- Prove it in an artefact: Ready should check must-have dependencies (the DB).
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not include optional vendors in ready.
- Prove it in an artefact: Keep probes cheap.
- Prove it in an artefact: Give boot a start grace.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not put secrets in the health body.

For each bullet, write pass or fail and the evidence. If every bullet is "pass" only because you nodded, you skipped the drill. Swap in a broken input and confirm the failure mode section still holds.

## What interviewers follow up with

After the definition they ask for the next action: which log, which status, which pin, which eval. Keep the 30-second line ready (Live means the process is up; ready means it can take traffic. I expose both, I SELECT 1 the database on ready, and I do not depend on a flaky vendor. The platform uses ready to hold traffic during boot) and immediately attach a number, a command, or a refusal. Do not invent a tool, a benchmark, or a vendor feature you have not used. If you do not know the exact API, say what you would read first and what mistake you are trying to avoid.

Close with the failure you would ship if you rushed: the one from the list above that looks like progress (green tests that never hit the bug, a cheaper model that fails the schema, a force-push that rewrites shared history).
keyPoints: Liveness: process is not dead. Readiness: safe to send traffic.
Ready should check must-have dependencies (the DB).
Do not include optional vendors in ready.
Keep probes cheap.
Give boot a start grace.
Do not put secrets in the health body.

questions.q: What is the difference between liveness and readiness?
questions.a: Liveness: the process should be restarted if it fails. Readiness: stop sending traffic until the app can actually serve (DB up, booted).

questions.q: What should /health/ready check for this capstone?
questions.a: That the process can reach Postgres (SELECT 1). Optionally that migrations are at head. Not an LLM vendor.

questions.q: The platform sends traffic during migrate and users see 500s. What is missing?
questions.a: A ready probe that fails until migrate finishes, plus a start grace period.

questions.q: Should ready fail if OpenAI is down?
questions.a: Only if the product cannot work at all without it. For a no-AI capstone, no. Even for an AI app, consider degraded mode.

questions.q: Why keep health public?
questions.a: The load balancer must reach it without a user token. Keep the body boring.

image-tags-vs-latest.explain:
## What it is

A **tag** is a name on an image: `tickets:1.2.0`. **`latest`** is just a tag that **moves**. It is not a magic pointer to "whatever is newest on the registry you think". If you deploy `latest`, you cannot say what digest is running, and a rebuild can change it under you.

**Pin a version tag** you created, or better a **digest** (`tickets@sha256:...`). CI builds `1.2.0` from a git SHA. Prod refers to that. Rollback is the previous tag. `latest` is fine on a laptop compose file if you understand it is sloppy; it is not fine in production.

The same rule as `uv.lock`: names that move are not reproducible.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, "prod is latest" is how two nodes run different code. Interviewers ask why latest is not reproducible and what you would pin. They ask how you roll back (previous tag). They ask the difference between a tag and a digest (a tag can be overwritten; a digest is content-addressed).

This is a short topic with a high signal.

## How it works + one small example

```
docker build -t ghcr.io/you/tickets:1.2.0 -t ghcr.io/you/tickets:git-a1b2c3d .
docker push ghcr.io/you/tickets:1.2.0
```

Deploy spec: `image: ghcr.io/you/tickets:1.2.0` or the digest the push printed.

CI can also tag `1.2.0` and `main`. Prod uses the version. Do not retag `1.2.0` to a new build; bump the version.

`docker pull tickets:latest` on two days can yield two images. That is the bug.

## Failure modes

1. **Prod = latest.**

2. **Retagging 1.2.0** to a new build.

3. **No git SHA** on the image, so you cannot say what code is live.

4. **Assuming the registry's latest matches your laptop's latest.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

latest moves. I pin a version tag or a digest, I never retag a released version, and I roll back by deploying the previous tag. Reproducible deploys are the same idea as a lockfile.

## Practice without a laptop story

Explain the idea out loud, then immediately give a counter-example where a nearby idea would have been the wrong fix. That is the interview shape: not "what is X" but "why not Y". Write the counter-example down. If you cannot name Y, you have only memorised a label.

Then bind the idea to evidence:

- Prove it in an artefact: latest is a moving tag, not a version.
- Prove it in an artefact: Pin a version tag or a digest in production.
- Prove it in an artefact: Do not overwrite a released tag.
- Prove it in an artefact: Put a git SHA on the image.
- Prove it in an artefact: Rollback = previous pin.
- Prove it in an artefact: Same idea as uv.lock.

Pick one reminder and implement the smallest proof: a unit test, a failing curl, a token count, a migration file, or a model-card quote. Time-box it to fifteen minutes. If it takes a day, the example in this note is still too abstract — shrink the domain (one table, one route, one prompt) and try again.

## The line and the leftover risk

The 30-second version is: latest moves. I pin a version tag or a digest, I never retag a released version, and I roll back by deploying the previous tag. Reproducible deploys are the same idea as a lockfile. The leftover risk is whatever that sentence does not mention — usually an adjacent failure (blocked event loop, leaked secret, silent truncation, contaminated benchmark, unpinned model). Name that leftover risk before you sit down. Interviewers score the leftover, not the slogan.

If you are teaching this to a teammate, have them break a working example on purpose and watch the exact symptom. The symptom is what you will recognise on call.
keyPoints: latest is a moving tag, not a version.
Pin a version tag or a digest in production.
Do not overwrite a released tag.
Put a git SHA on the image.
Rollback = previous pin.
Same idea as uv.lock.

questions.q: Why is latest not reproducible?
questions.a: It can be moved to a new image at any time. Two pulls can get two different digests.

questions.q: What do you put in the production deploy spec?
questions.a: A version tag you will not overwrite, or an image digest. Plus the env vars.

questions.q: Two replicas serve different behaviour but both say latest. Cause?
questions.a: They pulled at different times. Pin a digest so they cannot drift.

questions.q: How do you roll back 1.2.1?
questions.a: Deploy 1.2.0 (or its digest). You cannot if 1.2.0 was overwritten.

questions.q: Tag versus digest?
questions.a: A tag is a mutable name. A digest is the content hash of the image.

interview.explain:
## What it is

You will be asked to **debug a container that exits 1**. The walk-through is: **read the logs**, check the **CMD**, check **env vars**, check whether the **port is bound** on `0.0.0.0`. That order solves most capstone failures. You do not start by rewriting the Dockerfile.

They may add a twist: works locally with compose, dies on the platform. Then you add hops (health, secrets, tag). Keep the first four steps anyway.

Talk out loud. Name what you would type.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the Level 0 ship interview. It tests whether you have run `docker logs`. A candidate who says "I would rebuild" without reading logs has not shipped. On the job this is every deploy.

Pair it with the pytest interview: isolate, then change.

## How it works + one small example

Talk track:

1. `docker ps -a` — exit code, how long it lived.
2. `docker logs` — import error, missing env, traceback.
3. CMD — is uvicorn in the foreground? `0.0.0.0`? Right module path?
4. Env — is `DATABASE_URL` set in *this* environment? `docker inspect` if needed.
5. Port — EXPOSE vs `-p` vs listen address. curl from inside (`docker exec`) then from outside.

If logs show `ModuleNotFoundError: app`, COPY is wrong. If `KeyError: DATABASE_URL`, env is wrong. If nothing listens, CMD or bind is wrong.

Then: fix the image or the run flags, not the running container, and say how you would prevent it (ready probe, fail at boot).

## Failure modes

1. **Rebuild without logs.**

2. **SSH folklore** instead of logs/inspect.

3. **Fixing with exec** and calling it done.

4. **Ignoring the listen address.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Exits 1: logs, CMD, env, bind address. I name the commands, I fix the image or the run flags, and I do not exec a snowflake. Most ship bugs are a missing env or 127.0.0.1.

## How you would check this tomorrow

Do not stop at the definition. Pick one real artefact — a test, a log line, a header, a model card field, a Dockerfile layer, a curl transcript, or a SQL EXPLAIN — and use it to prove or disprove the claim. Write three things before you merge or answer: the artefact you will look at, the failure you expect if you skip the check, and the one-line note you would leave for the next person. Then run the check once with your own names, not the example names above.

Use these reminders as the working checklist:

- Prove it in an artefact: Order: logs → CMD → env → port/bind.
- Prove it in an artefact: Name the docker commands in the interview.
- Prove it in an artefact: Build success is not run success.
- Prove it in an artefact: Fix the image or run flags, not a snowflake exec.
- Prove it in an artefact: 127.0.0.1 and missing env are the usual causes.
- Prove it in an artefact: Prevent with fail-at-boot and ready probes.

If you cannot point at evidence, you do not know it yet. Re-read the example, change the identifiers, and redo it. A slide that only restates the 30-second line is not a check.

## Interview traps

Interviewers punish two moves: reciting a glossary without a decision, and claiming a tool just works. They will hand you a broken traceback, a status code, a latency number, a lockfile, or a model card and wait for the next action. Say what you look at first, what you change, and what you refuse to ship. If time is short, use this line and then add one concrete artefact: Exits 1: logs, CMD, env, bind address. I name the commands, I fix the image or the run flags, and I do not exec a snowflake. Most ship bugs are a missing env or 127.0.0.1.

A third trap is mixing adjacent ideas. Keep this topic's mechanism separate from nearby ones, name the trade-off, and give a number or a verb (measure, pin, retry, refuse) so the answer sounds like work, not a blog post.
keyPoints: Order: logs → CMD → env → port/bind.
Name the docker commands in the interview.
Build success is not run success.
Fix the image or run flags, not a snowflake exec.
127.0.0.1 and missing env are the usual causes.
Prevent with fail-at-boot and ready probes.

questions.q: Walk through debugging a container that exits 1.
questions.a: ps -a for the exit, logs for the traceback, inspect CMD and env, check it listens on 0.0.0.0. Fix the Dockerfile or run flags and recreate.

questions.q: Which four things does this prompt name?
questions.a: Logs, CMD, env vars, and whether the port is bound.

questions.q: Logs are empty and the container exited 0. What do you suspect?
questions.a: CMD returned immediately — a shell that ended, or a backgrounded server. Put the server in the foreground.

questions.q: It runs in compose and exits on the platform. What extra do you check?
questions.a: Secrets actually injected, image tag/digest, health checks, and the listen port the platform expects.

questions.q: Why not start with a rewrite of the Dockerfile?
questions.a: You do not yet know which layer failed. Logs usually name it in one line.
